activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Sarah had been at the community center every Tuesday and Thursday since September, first for open gym and then, when the rec league needed a fifth, for the volleyball team that practiced in the echoing gym with the cracked scoreboard. Her father had wanted her to find something structured before college, some discipline to inculcate a routine into her last summer at home, and she had agreed mostly to stop the conversation. Now it was October, and the season was down to three games, and Priya had a doctor's note folded into her sock.

Priya had taken a ball to the temple two weeks earlier, off Sarah's own serve, a shank that nobody could have called. Since then she had come back in stages, and Sarah had learned the shape of it almost without meaning to. First Priya only watched, sitting on the folded mats with the lights dimmed for her. Then she did light jogging along the sideline. Then, last Thursday, she was cleared for the non-contact drills, and tonight she was supposed to try actual play, scrimmaging, the last step before full games.

"Read my note if you want," Priya said, pulling it out of her sock in the hallway by the water fountain. "It says every step, rest to full play, and I only move up if I stay free of symptoms the whole way. One headache and I drop back down." Sarah read it twice. The paper was soft from being carried.

They were eleven minutes into the scrimmage when Sarah noticed Priya standing still at the net, one hand pressed to her eyebrow. Not hurt the way a rolled ankle hurts, but paused, the way you pause in a library. Sarah called the ball early, took the set herself, and put it down flat so the rally ended. Then she walked over.

"Head?"

"Kind of," Priya said. "Started when I tracked Dara's serve. It's not bad."

Coach Reyes blew the whistle and came over, arms crossed, and Sarah watched him weigh it. They needed tonight. Thursday was the semifinal, and Priya was their only real blocker, and everyone on the court knew it. "If it's not bad," he said slowly, "you could sit five and see."

Sarah heard the offer for what it was, and it wasn't dishonest, exactly, but it was specious, a reasonable-sounding cover for wanting her on the floor. She thought of her father, who had argued last week that a promise to yourself was the only contract nobody else could break, and of Priya's note, which said the opposite in a way: that you advanced only when nothing in you objected. For a second the two ideas sat side by side in her head, neither one winning.

"It says while," Sarah said. "You move up only while you're symptom free. Not five minutes of being symptom free." She hadn't planned to say it out loud, and she felt Reyes's eyes on her, but Priya was already nodding, already reaching for her knee pads' strap.

"I know," Priya said. "I go back a stage. Light drills, no scrimmage." She looked at Reyes, and something in her face made the decision hers, which Sarah understood was the only way it could stand. Reyes exhaled through his nose, then shrugged, and told Dara to switch to the net.

After practice Sarah helped Priya carry the ball cart to the equipment closet, because Priya wasn't supposed to lift much yet and because it was a small thing that cost Sarah nothing. They stood in the hallway under the humming fluorescent panel while Priya re-read her own note.

"I'll be honest," Sarah said. "I don't know if the doctor's way is right about everything. Maybe you'd have been fine. Maybe five minutes' rest fixes it and nobody knows." Priya tilted her head, considering, not arguing. "But you're the one who has to live in your head all year," Sarah went on, "and I only have to live with losing Thursday. That math seems pretty easy."

Priya laughed, folded the note, and slid it back into her sock. In the gym, Reyes was killing the lights one bank at a time, and the last square of brightness shrank toward the door where the two of them stood.

"Walk me out," Priya said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Gabrielle arrived at the farmers' market with her grandmother's canvas bag, forty dollars of her own babysitting money, and a plan she had defended at the kitchen table the night before. Her father wanted spaghetti and meatballs, the same dinner they had eaten every Sunday since she could remember, a tradition she privately considered parochial, as though the family palate had stopped exploring somewhere around 1998. She wanted to cook the pork loin from the Hsu farm stand, with the plums and the rosemary, the recipe she had torn from a magazine and taped inside her notebook like a confession. In the end she bought both, because in her family refusing anyone anything was a kind of arson.

She moved through the stalls with purpose, joking with Mr. Alvarez about whether his tomatoes were as good as he claimed, and letting him eviscerate a competitor's melons with one raised eyebrow. She counted her change. She argued herself down from the flowers and then, at the last stall, argued herself back up. By eleven she was carrying pork, plums, rosemary, a bag of tomatoes "for the meatballs, in case," and a terrible confidence that dinner would prove something, though she could not have said what.

Her brother Theo had left for college in August, and he texted while she was waiting in line for bread. "Cooking the family meal? Who are you and what have you done with my sister." Then, a second message: "Seriously though. Dad will say it's too fancy. Mom will say it's delicious to spite him. Report back." She read it twice, smiling, and did not answer yet, because answers felt like promises.

She cooked in the late afternoon with the kitchen windows open, the plums collapsing into the pan, the pork seared and then resting under foil. Her mother drifted through and stole a plum. Her father drifted through and said, "Smells like a restaurant," which in his dialect could mean anything. He changed his mind before dinner, though, out loud, at the table, which for him was practically opera. "This," he said, pointing his fork at the plums, "is better than the meatballs. Don't tell the meatballs." Everyone laughed, even Gabrielle, even the dog, who was hoping to be consulted.

Afterward they sat on the back porch in the blue evening, and it was hot, the kind of hot where the porch swing complained and the lemonade went watery. The platters came out with them, because no one wanted to go back inside, and the pork sat in its juices on the table while they argued about whether Aunt Rosa's new boyfriend was truly terrible or just boring, a debate with a long and distinguished history. Gabrielle looked at the meat and felt a small cold thought arrive.

She went inside and found the thermometer magnet on the fridge, the one from a food safety pamphlet her mother had never read. Her phone was faster. She searched, and there it was, plain as arithmetic: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or for more than one hour when it's above 90. She read it twice. She stepped back onto the porch, where the air itself felt like a held breath, thick and ninety-something, and looked at the clock inside her own head. They had been out here longer than one hour. Longer than two.

"Everything's done," she said, gathering the platters, and her father said, "Done?" and she said, "Done for. The meat. It's been sitting out in this heat, and the rule is two hours in the danger zone, one hour if it's over ninety, and we are way past one." Her mother said, "The danger zone," slowly, as though tasting the phrase. "That sounds like a movie your brother would like." Gabrielle scraped the pork and the plums into the trash while her father mourned quietly and dramatically, one hand on his chest, and the dog watched the garbage can with frank theological despair.

Later, alone in the kitchen, she washed the pan and thought about her grandmother, who had raised five kids on leftovers and prayer and would have laughed at the waste, and about Theo's food science textbooks, which he quoted at dinner like scripture. Two inheritances, and she could hold both, she decided, roughly; she would trust the thermometer and the rule, and she would cook less next time, and she would still not tell her grandmother. The plums had been perfect, though, and the pork was gone, and there was no version of tonight without that.

She texted Theo a photo of the empty trash can and the thermometer magnet. "You were right about the danger zone. Dad loved dinner and then I eviscerated it, per USDA. Consanguinity entitles you to half the blame for my cooking genes." She dried her hands and set the pan back on the stove, and outside, faintly, she could hear her father and the dog, negotiating over the last piece of bread.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
story:
Jackson had been volunteering at the Harbor Street Community Office for six weeks, and until Tuesday morning nobody had asked him to write anything.

Mrs. Adeyemi, the coordinator, called him over to the desk by the window. "I need a favor," she said. "Dara's out sick, and this email to the parks department has to go out by noon. The grant meeting is Thursday, and if we don't confirm the picnic shelter by then, we lose it." She slid a printout across the desk. "Read this and tell me what you think."

Jackson read it. Dara, the part-time staffer, had written a page and a half about the history of the summer program, the weather last July, a complaint about a broken water fountain, and then, in the final paragraph, a request to reserve the Riverside shelter on August 12. It meandered like a river deciding where to go. He could tell Dara was trying to sound professional, stacking formal phrases to burnish the message, but the polish hid the point instead of brightening it.

"It's polite," he said carefully. "It's just that the ask is buried."

"Can you fix it by eleven?" Mrs. Adeyemi was already halfway back to the phone, where a parent was asking about bus passes. "Keep it respectful. Mr. Okafor over there can be touchy about tone, so don't be blunt."

Jackson sat down at the volunteer computer. He typed a draft, deleted it, typed another. The question he kept circling was simple and stubborn: what did a professional voice actually sound like? He'd written school essays meant to impress a teacher, but this was different. Somebody on the other end had forty other emails and a shelter calendar, and the kindest thing might be to stop performing and just say the thing.

He was still rearranging paragraphs when Ren, the college intern, leaned over his shoulder with a granola bar. "What's the mess?"

"Trying to figure out where the request goes," Jackson said. "Dara put it last, like a reveal."

Ren chewed for a second. "My cousin's in the Navy. She drills this into everybody. 'Bottom Line Up Front', BLUF. It's a US military writing standard. You put the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details."

"So the ask goes first, and the reasons come after."

"Exactly. She says nobody overseas has time to hunt for the point."

Jackson turned back to the screen. It felt almost rude, like walking into someone's office and talking before saying hello. But maybe, he thought, leading with the request was a form of respect, an admission that the reader's time mattered. He wrote a new draft.

Dear Mr. Okafor,

I'm writing to confirm our reservation of the Riverside picnic shelter for August 12, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., for the Harbor Street summer program's family day, roughly 80 attendees.

If the shelter is available, could you reply by Wednesday so we can finalize the grant paperwork? Below is the background, in case it's useful.

He kept the history Dara had gathered but cut it to four sentences. He left out the water fountain complaint entirely, then second-guessed himself and added one line, since Dara had clearly wanted it mentioned: "Separately, we'd appreciate knowing when the drinking fountain near the east entrance might be repaired." Maybe that was wrong, mixing requests. Maybe it was honest. He couldn't decide, and he let it stand.

Mrs. Adeyemi read it at 11:20, her face dour with deadline worry until the second line, when it eased. "This is good. Short and clear." Then she paused. "The fountain thing. He'll read that as a criticism of his department."

"Is that bad? Dara wanted it on record."

"It's a question of whether we need the shelter more than we need the complaint." She handed it back. "Your call. You're the one writing it."

Jackson sat with it for a moment. Two instincts pulled at him: Dara's instinct to document everything, soften everything, wrap the point in velvet; and the BLUF instinct to state the point and get out of the way. Neither felt complete on its own. The email could be direct and still be generous. He moved the fountain line to the end, after the background, and reworded it: "One small unrelated note, no urgency: the drinking fountain near the east entrance has been out of service, and families would be glad when it's working again."

He hit send at 11:52.

At 2:40 the reply came. Mr. Okafor confirmed the shelter, said he'd have the permit signed by Wednesday morning, and added a single line about the fountain: a work order had been filed in June, and he would check on its status. Then, at the bottom: "Thank you for making your request easy to find."

Mrs. Adeyemi printed it and pinned it to the corkboard above the office printer. "Dara should see this when she's back," she said, and Jackson noticed she'd circled the last sentence in red pen.

He stood there a minute longer than he needed to, reading it again. He still didn't know whether he'd been right to keep the fountain line at all, or whether softening it had been wisdom or cowardice. That part stayed unresolved, the way real things did. But he copied the email into a file he labeled "forms and templates," and saved it under a new folder name: BLUF, and other things I don't know yet.

Ren passed by with the last of the granola bar. "So what's the verdict? Military style?"

"Half," Jackson said. "Blunt up front, polite at the back."

"Sounds like stoicism with manners," Ren said, and laughed.

Jackson didn't answer, but he wrote that down too.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
story:
The argument John had prepared was about heredity and choice. He had written it on two sides of an index card the night before: that a person's observable traits, the phenotype, set certain conditions, but that conditions were not commands, and that anyone who claimed genes dictated a life had skipped a step. He wanted to say it well. He had been quiet in this class since September, and Mr. Okafor had asked him twice, gently, whether he had thoughts he was saving for later. Today he had a card with him, and a raised hand, and the small honest want of a boy who wanted to be heard getting it right.

The discussion had already started when the bell stopped ringing. Marcus was talking, leaning back with his chair on two legs, about a magazine article claiming that scientists had proved people were born criminals. "So if your genes say you're going to steal," Marcus said, "punishment is basically pointless. That's the logical conclusion of the whole genetic position." A few people nodded. Someone near the window said, grimly, that he refused to believe humans were just meat programs.

John put his hand up and made his argument, reading partly from the card and partly from somewhere braver. He said the phenotype was a starting condition, like the terrain a road is built on, and that roads went many ways across the same terrain. He said the evidence for influence was not evidence for fate. When he finished, the room was quiet in a way he could not read, and then Marcus dropped his chair forward with a bang.

"So you're saying it doesn't matter how kids are raised," Marcus said. "If it's all in the genes anyway, then bad parents are off the hook, and we can just malign poor families for their DNA and call it science. That's what you're defending." He spread his hands, as though the conclusion were obvious and a little dirty. Around him, people were frowning, but the frowns were aimed at John now, at the ugly thing Marcus had placed in his mouth, something about eugenics and excuses, a position John had never taken and would never take.

"That's not what I said," John managed. His voice came out thinner than he wanted. "I said influence, not control." But Marcus was already talking over him, generously offering to agree to disagree, as if he had done John a favor by dismantling him. John looked down at his index card, at his own tidy handwriting, and felt the strange vertigo of being defeated by an argument that had never touched his own.

Across the room, Dana had stopped doodling. She had written down both claims in her notebook, in her cramped shorthand, one under the other: John's actual words, and Marcus's reply. The two did not match. Marcus had not answered the road built across terrain; he had answered something easier, a flimsier version standing where John had been standing, and he was swinging at it as though it were the same thing. She raised her hand, and when Mr. Okafor nodded to her, she turned toward Marcus rather than the teacher.

"That's a straw man," she said. "You attacked a weaker, distorted version of his argument instead of the argument he actually made, and you're acting like the two are the same." Marcus opened his mouth, and Dana pointed at her notebook, which was not a normal thing to do, and read John's sentence back verbatim, then read Marcus's rebuttal verbatim. "He said influence, not control," she said. "You answered control. If it's a fallacy, the whole reply just falls off the argument, like knocking over a dummy and claiming you beat the man." The class was very still. Marcus said, "Fine, then he should have been clearer," which was not the same as conceding, and everyone seemed to know it.

Mr. Okafor asked whether John wanted to respond, and John found that the moment had changed shape on him. He had planned for opposition, for a real counterargument about twin studies or free will, and what he had gotten instead was a distortion, which required a different move: not to defend his claim harder, but to first restore it, to say, "Before you argue with me, argue with me." He said that, almost exactly, and heard a couple of people laugh quietly, the good kind of laugh. Then he said the part he was less sure of, because it was true. "I don't actually know where influence ends," he said. "I know it's not everything. I can't tell you the percentage, and I don't think anyone in this room can. If you want to beat my real argument, that's the place to hit it, because that's where I'm standing."

Marcus looked at him for a long second, chair flat on the floor now, and then said, "All right. Say more about the percentage thing." John put the index card face down on his desk, because he was about to go off it, and started talking.

activity: graduating from high school
story:
Landon found the cap first, then the gown, then the tassel, in that order, in three different places: the cap under his bed, the gown on the laundry hook where it had been since March, the tassel in a mug on his desk that said WORLD'S OKAYEST FISHERMAN, a gift from an uncle who had never seen him fish. The ceremony was in nine hours. His mother was already in the kitchen making potato salad for the party, halving eggs with a serrated knife, which he had told her a hundred times was wrong and which she did anyway.

The problem was the speech. Two weeks earlier, when Mr. Ruiz had asked him to speak for the class, Landon had said yes because it was easier than saying no, and now he had a legal pad with four false starts on it and a fifth one that ended mid-sentence at the word "meanwhile." He had tried solemn. He had tried funny. Both had desiccated on the page, the jokes curling up like the edges of the eggs his mother was currently butchering. He sat at the kitchen table with the pad while she worked, and she did not ask about the speech, because she knew him well enough not to.

The party started at two, in the backyard, under a canopy his stepfather had borrowed from a man at work. People came in a slow tide: aunts, neighbors, kids Landon had known since trundle beds, kids he had met in eleventh grade and liked fine. Dana Okafor arrived with her grandmother and a casserole and the expression of someone surveying a land she had once ruled. Gus came late, as Gus did, carrying a basketball even though there was no game planned.

It was Gus, actually, standing at the drink table with a red cup, who said it. "Where's Ricky Solano? And those O'Malley twins. I figured they'd be here even if they didn't walk." He counted on his fingers, half joking, and then stopped counting because the list got longer than a joke could carry. "We started with like 340."

"There's, what, 290 walking tomorrow," Dana said. She had a way of saying numbers like she was handing you change. Landon watched her do the arithmetic in her head and then pull out her phone, because even Dana checked. She scrolled, frowned, scrolled again, and turned the screen toward them. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." She said it flat, like reading a train schedule. "That's the whole country, that year."

"So we're average," Gus said.

"We're a data point," said Dana, and put the phone away, and took a cupcake.

Landon had been drifting toward his own speech problem all afternoon, the way a loose tooth finds the tongue, and now he could not stop pressing on it. He walked to the far end of the yard, past the canopy, where the grass turned to dirt near the fence, and stood there doing what he always did with numbers: turning them into faces. Ricky Solano, who had moved junior year and sent one Snap after that. The O'Malley twins. A girl named Priya who had left mid-October of sophomore year without a word, whose locker he had watched get taped over and reassigned. Thirteen percent of somewhere. But that was the country, that year, not his class, and his class was not a fixed thing either, kids arriving and leaving like weather. He understood the statistic and did not understand his class, and he understood his class, in the face-by-face way, and could not fit it to the statistic, and both of those were true, and he stood in the dirt trying to hold them at once.

His mother found him there. "You're hiding," she said.

"I'm drafting."

"In the dirt."

"Where no one can see me delete things."

She looked at him for a moment, and there was a kind of clemency in it, the look she gave when she had decided not to say the thing she plainly wanted to say, which was that he could still call Mr. Ruiz and back out. "Potato salad's out," she said instead. "It has eggs in it. That's all I'll say."

Later, when the canopy lights came on and the yard shrank into its own small bright country, Gus stole the mic from the borrowed speaker, supposedly to lead a toast, mostly to stall for Landon. "Our valedictorian," Gus announced, mispronouncing it deliberately, "is still writing." A laugh moved through the tectonic shift of folding chairs, everyone turning toward Landon at the same geological speed.

He stood up. He did not have the legal pad. He had a sentence he had built walking back across the grass, and he knew only the first half of it. "Some of the people we started with aren't here," he said, "and some of them we could have called and didn't, and the numbers say that's ordinary, and I can't tell yet whether ordinary makes it better or worse." He stopped there. It was not an ending. Dana raised her red cup without a word, and after a second, everyone else did too, and Gus whispered, "Nine a.m., you're on," and turned the music back up.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
Mya found her father in the kitchen at six in the morning, standing before the cleared end of the counter with a shoebox of photographs and no idea what to do with it. The funeral had been in March, which meant her grandmother had been gone long enough that the grief had changed shape, become quieter and more portable, and now here was November arriving with its own demands. On the counter her father had already set a jar of marigolds he must have bought on his way home from the night shift, the orange almost too loud against the white tile.

"She liked the pan de muerto from the bakery on Cesar Chavez," he said, not turning around. "The one with the sesame seeds, not the sugar."

Mya hadn't known that. She knew her grandmother's coffee, black with too much sugar, and the way she could be bellicose about politics at the dinner table, going after uncles twice her size until somebody changed the subject to soccer. But the sweet bread, the specific bakery, the sesame versus the sugar, all of that belonged to her father's childhood, not to hers. He had grown up in this city with the grandmother; Mya had grown up three states away, visiting in summers, receiving birthday cards with five-dollar bills folded inside.

"Is this an altar?" she asked. "Like a real one?"

"An ofrenda," he said. "We build them November first and second. Day of the Dead. Photos, her favorite foods, her drinks. Whatever she loved."

He said it plainly, the way he said everything, and she understood he was not performing a tradition so much as returning to one, the way you return to a house you lived in as a child and find the light switches with your hands in the dark. Mya had been raised half in that house and half outside it. Her mother was from Ohio and had never vilified the old customs, exactly, but had a way of calling them "your father's side of things" that kept them at a certain distance, and Mya had let that distance stand because it was easier than learning what was on the other side of it.

She took the shoebox from the counter and sat at the table to go through it. The photos were curled and some had lost their corners. Her grandmother at thirty, squinting into sun. Her grandmother at the stove in this same kitchen, younger than Mya was now, holding a cast-iron pan. Her grandmother holding a baby who had to be her father. Mya tried to match the kitchen in the photograph to the kitchen around her, the window, the doorframe, and felt something she could only call synchronicity, two moments occupying the same few square feet of tile, forty years apart, herself the only witness to both.

"I should have come more," she said. "Last summer especially. She asked me to come help her can the tomatoes and I said I had a program."

Her father was quiet while he folded a cloth, cream-colored with embroidered edges, and laid it over a stack of boxes that had been in the garage. The cloth had to be older than either of them. "She knew you had a program," he said finally. "She told everybody at church her granddaughter had a program. She wasn't confused about it."

"But she asked anyway."

"She asked anyway." He set a framed photo on the cloth and studied it. "People ask anyway. That's mostly what asking is."

The bakery opened at seven. Mya drove because her father's eyes were tired from the shift, and she stood in line behind a woman buying four loaves and a tray of sugar skulls wrapped in cellophane. The bread was still warm when the baker handed it over, dusted with sesame, round with the little knobs of dough on top. In the car she held the bag on her lap and her father didn't say anything, and she thought about how a person could keep existing in bread, in a folded cloth, in the specific absence of sugar on a crust, long after the funeral, and how she still couldn't decide whether that was comfort or just the shape a missing person leaves.

Back in the kitchen she set the loaf on the cloth beside the coffee cup, the good one with the gold rim, filled with black coffee and too much sugar. Her father placed the photograph of the grandmother at the stove, and Mya added the one of the baby, and they stepped back at the same moment. Then her father went to answer his phone in the other room, and Mya stood alone in front of the ofrenda with the marigolds and the bread and the two photographs, and she said, out loud, "I'll come next summer. I'll help with the tomatoes." She reached forward and turned the coffee cup a quarter turn, so the gold rim faced the window and the morning light caught it.

story:
The gallery was cold in the way of rooms that guard their canvases more carefully than their visitors, and Marcus stood in front of a painting of nested squares with his sketchbook clamped under one arm. He had come because Ms. Rothenberg had said his portfolio application needed a theme, ten pieces that spoke to each other, and he had said "fine" in the tone he used when he meant the opposite. Now he wrote in his sketchbook, "squares? boring?" and crossed it out.

"You've been standing there for ten minutes," said Priya, appearing beside him with her coat still on. They had applied to the same summer intensive, and though they had never quite called themselves friends, they had fallen into the habit of being honest with each other because it was easier than performing.

"Ten minutes," Marcus said. "Ten pieces. I keep counting."

Priya leaned in and read the wall label. "Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976. Keeping the nested squares constant while changing only the colours." She said it flatly, like reading a bus schedule, and then looked at him. "A thousand. For twenty-six years. Same squares."

"That's the part I can't get past." Marcus turned his sketchbook toward her so she could see the page, which held, instead of drawings, a list of themes he had considered and abandoned: doors, his grandmother's hands, the river by the train tracks, each one crossed out with a different weight of pen. "I keep thinking a theme means finding something profound. He just picked a shape and stayed."

"Maybe staying is the profound part."

He didn't answer, because a docent was shepherding a cluster of middle-schoolers past them, and one of the kids said, loudly, that anyone could paint squares, and the docent laughed in a way that agreed. Marcus felt an old defensiveness rise, the same one he'd felt two years ago in Mr. Ito's studio class when a boy named Devon had called Marcus's color studies "easy" and Marcus had thrown away three weeks of work rather than let them be maligned. He had regretted that for a long time, though he had never said so to anyone. The torn canvases had gone out with the recycling on a Tuesday, and he had watched the truck take them, and had told himself it was about standards.

Outside the museum, the January light was the flat white of an unwritten page. Priya unwrapped a granola bar and split it without being asked, which was how she apologized for things she wouldn't name. "So say you did it," she said. "Same composition, ten times, one thing different each time. What's your one thing?"

"Colour," Marcus said, and then heard himself and laughed. "Which is just doing Albers again."

"Doing Albers again is also over a thousand pieces deep. You'd be doing it once." She chewed and looked at the traffic on Bloor Street. "It's a truism that you have to find your own voice, but nobody says the voice might start as someone else's mouth moving."

He wrote that down, because it was better than anything on his list. "My grandmother's kitchen," he said slowly. "It's yellow. It's been yellow my whole life. Except it hasn't, not really, it's been six different yellows, and I only noticed when my uncle painted it that grey-blue last spring and she hated it so much she cried." He was talking faster now, his cold breath visible. "Same kitchen. Same window over the sink, same table. Only the colour changing, and it changed whether the whole room felt like hers."

Priya stopped chewing. "That's not squares."

"No. But it's the method." He flipped to a clean page and drew a quick rectangle, the kitchen, and nested inside it the window, and inside the window whatever was outside. He drew it four times, small, and wrote above each one a different word: mustard, cream, the grey-blue, and one he left blank. "It's parsimonious," he said, half apologizing, "but maybe that's not bad. One decision, repeated, and every difference means something because the composition isn't fighting for attention."

"That word sounds like an insult."

"It's the opposite." He looked at the four rectangles, then across the street at a building whose windows were reflecting a colour of sky he couldn't name, and realized he was already mixing it in his head, and that the blank word would have to stay blank for now, because he did not yet know what his grandmother's kitchen would become, or whether she would ever forgive the grey-blue, or whether ten pieces could hold a thing he understood only as a feeling in a room. "I'm going to need her to send me photographs," he said. "Before and after."

The gym smelled like rubber and cold air, and Florence had the ball at the top of the key with eleven seconds left in a scrimmage nobody was supposed to care about. She cared. She had missed her last four shots, every one rattling off the back rim, and now Coach Voss was yelling from the sideline, "Swing it, Flo, swing it," because everyone on the floor believed the same thing: a girl who has missed four in a row will miss the fifth.

She swung it. The possession died in a travel call, and practice ended with wind sprints that left her lungs burning, and in the locker room afterward Priya was talking again, the way she talked after every loss, calmly, like she was reading from a spreadsheet only she could see. "There's no such thing as the hot hand," Priya said, lacing her shoes. "It's a bias. The original study proved it in 1985."

Florence pulled her sweatshirt over her head. "Proved what, exactly?"

"That shooters don't get hot. That a made shot doesn't make the next one more likely." Priya said it the way other people said water is wet. She was the one who kept a notebook of every shot anyone took in practice, makes and misses in tidy columns, and she had chosen Florence's name in the draft two seasons ago because, she said, Florence's percentages were the most stable on the team. It had not sounded like a compliment. It had sounded like being called a machine.

The problem was that Florence did not feel like a machine. She felt hot sometimes. There were nights when the rim looked enormous, when her release felt predicated on nothing but her own certainty, and the ball went where she decided it would go, three or four or five times running, and the whole gym seemed to lean toward her. Those nights were the reason she loved the game. Priya's notebook made those nights sound like weather, like luck, like nothing she had earned.

She started keeping her own count that week, in the margins of her stats homework. Makes and misses, same as Priya, except she wrote hers after the fact from memory, and the two records never matched, which bothered her more than it probably should have. Thursday, Priya cornered her by the water fountain with the notebook open and said, "You're shooting thirty-eight percent in practice and fifty-two in games. Do you understand how weird that is?" Florence said she didn't, and Priya said, "Neither do I," which was the first time Florence had ever heard her admit such a thing.

The argument broke open on Saturday, in front of everyone. Coach Voss had benched Jess for taking a heat-check three early in the shot clock, and Jess had muttered something on the bench, and Priya, stretching on the floor, had said, not unkindly, "He's right. The hot hand isn't real. It's been studied." Coach Voss stopped stacking cones. "I've coached twenty years," he said. "I've seen it. You'll see it too, if you last in this game long enough." Priya stood up and, to her lasting credit, did not raise her voice. "The 1985 study was wrong, though. It had a flaw in the math. Two economists, Miller and Sanjurjo, they found the bias in 2018." She said it flat, no drama. "They rechecked the old data and found evidence of streak shooting in it. Same data. So the hot hand is real."

The gym went quiet the way gyms do, with a ball bouncing once somewhere and nobody chasing it. Coach Voss looked at Priya for a long moment and then said, "Then we're both right," and turned back to his cones, and everyone laughed except Florence, because she was busy holding the two ideas at arm's length and turning them. The old study said no. The newer one said yes, in the same numbers, once the bias was taken out. It wasn't relativism, she decided, not really; it wasn't a case of everyone getting their own truth. It was a case of a measurement being wrong and then being corrected, which meant the truth had been there the whole time, waiting for someone to count it properly. What stayed uncertain was her. Whether her hot nights were the real thing Miller and Sanjurjo had found evidence of, or just Priya's weather, she could not know from the inside. She could not ever know from the inside.

Priya found her after practice, at the door, and held out the notebook, open to a page of Florence's recent practices. The columns had a new mark in them, small circles around stretches of consecutive makes. "I don't know what I think yet," Priya said. "But I stopped pretending I did. You had six in a row on Tuesday. I circled it because if the effect is real, it should show up somewhere, and you're the one whose numbers I'd trust to show it." Florence looked at the circles. There were three of them on the page, small and precise, and something in her chest loosened, the way it loosened when a pass arrived exactly on time.

"That's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about my field goal percentage," Florence said.

"It's not nice, it's method," Priya said, but she was almost smiling, and she zipped the notebook into her bag and held the door.

The next game, late in the fourth quarter, Florence missed twice, then made three in a row, and on the fourth possession she caught the ball at the wing with nobody open, and Coach Voss was shouting swing it, and Priya was on her feet at the end of the bench, and Florence rose anyway, the rim enormous, and let it go.

story:
The Kellers' basement smelled like microwave popcorn and wet rain jackets, and by halftime eleven people were crowded onto furniture meant for six. Nevaeh had the corner of the couch, the good seat, because she'd arrived early to help Mr. Keller carry the cooler downstairs. On the screen, Darnell Pryor had made five shots in a row for the second game straight, and the basement had split into two camps.

"He's on fire," said Marcus, Mr. Keller's son, standing up so fast he knocked over a can of root beer. "You don't leave a hot player on the bench. That's just basketball."

Nevaeh's father, two seats over, waved his cup. "It's the hot hand fallacy, kid. Somebody proved it. Back in the eighties." He looked around the room the way he did when he wanted someone to ask who.

"Who," said Nevaeh, flat, because she knew it would make him prevaricate, start in on his college days at Michigan State instead of the actual study. He did, for a minute, something about a statistics professor and a bar argument, and then he lost the thread, and the room went back to the game while Pryor missed his next two shots. Marcus pointed at the screen like a prosecutor resting his case.

Later that night, unable to sleep, Nevaeh looked it up on her phone under her blanket. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985. They had called the hot hand an illusion. She read the phrase twice, then kept scrolling, because something about it bothered her, the same feeling she got when a proof in calculus looked finished and wasn't. Somewhere further down she found the other thing: a reanalysis in 2018 by two researchers named Miller and Sanjurjo, who had found a flaw in the original statistics, and evidence of streak shooting. Two studies, thirty-three years apart, saying opposite things about the same game. She fell asleep with the phone on her chest.

She remembered the fourth grade, then, before she'd meant to: her mother on the porch steps, before the divorce, before the apartment on Deloit Street, explaining why she was leaving. Not explaining, really. She'd said "your father and I want different things," and even at nine Nevaeh had understood that this was a way of saying nothing while sounding like something. Her mother could prevaricate beautifully. Maybe that was where Nevaeh got her habit of not trusting any single story, or maybe that was solipsism, believing she'd invented the whole pattern herself. She couldn't tell. That was the part she hated, that she couldn't tell.

Saturday morning she walked back to the Kellers' with a printout folded in her jacket pocket. Marcus was in the driveway shooting at a bent rim nailed to the garage, which was what Marcus did most mornings, because Marcus wanted a Division One scholarship more than he had ever wanted anything, and because his father wanted it more than that.

"Your dad thinks Pryor's just lucky," she said, catching his rebound and handing it back.

"My dad thinks Coach Rice should bench him. My dad's mad because his fantasy team lost." Marcus shot, missed, retrieved. "Everybody's got a reason they like."

She held out the printout. "There were two studies," she said. "The old one, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985, said the hot hand was an illusion. But in 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo redid it and found a statistical flaw. And evidence of streak shooting."

Marcus took the paper and read it standing in the driveway with the ball under one arm. His lips moved a little on "reanalysis." A car went past with its windows down, someone's music, then quiet again.

"So who's right?" he said finally.

"Both of them were doing math. The math was wrong once and then it was less wrong." She shoved her hands in her pockets. "I think maybe Pryor is actually streaky. But I don't know if he's going to make the next shot. Nobody knows that. Not even Pryor."

"That's the worst answer I've ever heard."

"It's the only true one."

Marcus looked at the paper again, then folded it and put it in his waistband, which meant he was keeping it, which meant something. He bounced the ball twice and shot from the driveway's cracked seam, the same spot he'd missed from a minute before. It went in without touching the rim.

He turned around and grinned at her, arms spread.

The cold came up through the concrete of the stadium benches in a way Jaxon had not expected, as if the whole structure were anchored in winter somewhere far below. He sat wedged between his father and his uncle Ray, with his cousin Marisol two seats down, and above them the December sky hung gray and motionless over the field. It was the first time his father's side and his mother's side had shared tickets to anything, a happenstance born of a canceled family reunion and a cousin who worked in the athletic office, and so far the experiment was holding. Uncle Ray had brought a thermos of coffee strong enough to strip paint, and he offered it around at every timeout as a kind of diplomacy.

The game had captivated even Jaxon, who had come mainly to keep the peace. He did not care who won, but he had begun to care about the shape of the contest itself, the way momentum tilted and held, the arithmetic of field position. His father, a quiet man at games, leaned forward with his hands folded against his mouth like a shield. Marisol kept a running commentary that was smarter than the broadcasters'.

Then, early in the third quarter, the running back broke free along the sideline, twisted at the goal line, and the side judge threw his flag even as the back judge waved his arms to signal the touchdown. From their angle it was impossible to say whether the ball had crossed the plane before the runner's knee touched. The stadium screens showed the live shot and then, maddeningly, a commercial. Around them, sixty thousand people began to shout for a replay, and Uncle Ray stood up among them, choleric and red-faced, bellowing at the nearest camera operator on the field, "Show it again! Show it again, you cowards!"

The call went to review, and the referee announced it in that flat, ritual way officials have, but the jumbotron still showed nothing. "It wasn't like this before," Ray grumbled as he sat back down. "In my day they just called it and you lived with it. You lived with it or you got thrown out." He said this as though it were a virtue, and Jaxon's father said nothing, which was his way of disagreeing.

"It had to start somewhere," Marisol said. "Somebody had to be first." Jaxon found that he knew this, and knew it precisely, though he could not immediately say where from. A documentary, he realized, one he had watched alone over the summer at two in the morning, half asleep, the kind of programming that fills the hours when no one is watching. He had assumed he would forget it by morning, and instead it surfaced now, entire, like something raised from the bottom of a lake.

"The first instant replay on TV was during the Army-Navy game," he said. "December seventh, nineteen sixty-three. CBS showed it." His father lowered his shield of hands and looked at him. "A director came up with the system," Jaxon went on, more carefully now, because the memory was still assembling itself as he spoke. "Tony Verna." Uncle Ray squinted at him, and for a moment Jaxon thought he was about to be mocked for storing such a thing. Instead Ray said, "Army-Navy. My father watched that game every year," and something in his voice loosened, as if the fact had reached backward through the decades and touched someone Jaxon had never met.

They argued, after that, about whether the replay had been good for the game or bad for it. Ray held that doubt was now everybody's permanent condition, that no call was ever accepted, that the stadium had become a courtroom. Marisol argued the opposite, that knowing was better than believing, even when the knowing hurt. Jaxon listened to both of them and found he could not land entirely on either side. He wanted the truth of the play, and he also wanted, in some older part of himself, the world his great-grandfather had watched, where the game happened once, live, and then was gone, and you argued about it at dinner for years because there was nothing else to do with it. Both of those things seemed true to him and they did not fit together, and he could not resolve it, and he noticed, with a strange small satisfaction, that he did not much want to.

The referee came back on the field, lifted his microphone, and said the ruling on the field stood. Touchdown. Half the stadium roared and half of it went hollow with outrage, and Uncle Ray threw his cap to the ground between his feet, where it sat there looking stunned. The jumbotron finally, belatedly, showed the play once, at full speed, from the one angle that settled nothing. "That's it?" Ray shouted at it. "That's what we waited for?" Marisol laughed and pulled the cap off the ground and set it back on his head, tamping it down with both hands like she was crowning him.

story:
Abigail signed out the classroom kitchen for four o'clock on Friday because her mother had picked up doubles at the hospital and somebody had to feed Danny. She laid out the tomatoes and the cheap cut of beef on the steel counter, next to the recipe card she'd copied from her grandmother's handwriting, and tried not to think about how the card assumed a kitchen that no longer existed, in a city far below this one. Danny had insisted on coming, and he set his igneous rock on the counter like a paperweight, the chunk of speckled stone he'd pried out of the trail behind the new house and carried everywhere for a week.

Above the stove somebody had taped a chart, curling at the corners, headed HIGH ALTITUDE ADJUSTMENTS. Mrs. Otero had handed out copies the first week of term and Abigail had filed hers without reading it, because the school sat in a valley town and the chart seemed meant for skiers, for people with cabins, for a life that was not hers. She cooked the sauce low and slow, tasted it against the memory of her grandmother's version, and portioned out pasta for the night, everything timed so it would take eleven minutes at a rolling boil, which was what the box said.

Up the mountain, in the house that still smelled of paint, the water took forever to heat and then broke into its boil all at once. Danny stood at her elbow with the thermometer from his science kit because he liked gadgets more than he liked being told to set the table. She slid the pasta in at 6:12 and set the timer. At 6:23 she pulled a strand, blew on it, bit it, and bit it again. It cracked between her teeth like a promise.

"It's hard," Danny said.

"It's not hard. It's al dente."

"It's hard, Abigail."

She turned the burner higher, which did nothing, because the water was already doing everything water at a boil could do, and both of them stood there watching pale noodles knock against the pot. Danny said something about how their mom was going to come home to gravel for dinner after working fourteen hours, and Abigail told him to go watch his show, and he went, dragging his rock along the counter on purpose, and the clang of it in the hallway was very loud.

She nearly texted her mother. She had the message drafted, something about ordering pizza, but she deleted it, because the whole point of tonight had been that her mother would walk in and sit down and be fed by somebody else for once. Instead she opened her binder on the counter and found Mrs. Otero's handout, soft from being carried for two months, and flattened it under the salt shaker and read it while the noodles sat stubborn in their water. Then she called Danny back in.

"Read that," she said.

He read it slowly, the way he read everything. "Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook."

"Are we at 5,000 feet?"

"The sign at the turnoff says so. Every time."

"Then put the thermometer in."

The water, boiling hard, roared as hot as it was ever going to get, and the thermometer held just under 95. Danny watched the number like it was a score. In calculus they'd spent a month learning to parametrize a curve, to let some third variable stand behind the familiar two and pull them along, and Abigail understood now that the recipe card was the same kind of incomplete object, that it had been written for a lower world and she'd been following it as if nothing had changed. She dropped the pasta back in, set the timer for nine more minutes, and when Danny asked what he could do, she didn't tell him to leave.

"You can stir," she said. "And the fight about the rock, and the gravel. Amnesty."

"That's for wars."

"Dinner's a war."

He stirred, carefully, twice in each direction, and reported the temperature at every check as though it might suddenly betray them again. The second strand bent and gave, soft all the way through, and the sauce had kept warm on the back of the stove where she'd moved it without thinking, which was the kind of small rightness she decided not to examine. They heard the car at 7:40, gravel and headlights, and Abigail drained the pot and plated while Danny put out forks for three.

Her mother came in with her jacket still on, stopped at the smell of it, and sat down. Abigail set the plate in front of her and then her own beside it, and Danny said, "It took nine extra minutes because of the mountain," and reached for the Parmesan.

story:
Anthony had promised his grandmother a set for her tea, and he intended to keep the promise before the summer ended. In his grandfather's workshop behind the house, a converted carriage house that smelled of wet dust and linseed oil, there were two shelves of clay, and he had chosen without thinking much about it. The smaller bag, dense and pale, had come from the college supply in the city. The larger one, reddish and sandy, was the old kind his grandfather had used for decades. Anthony wedged both, threw a slender cup from the pale clay and a wide bowl from the red, and set them together on the board by the window, where the arboreal shade of the backyard oaks moved across them all afternoon.

The kiln log changed things. He found it while looking for witness cones, a school notebook with a cracked spine, decades of firings recorded in his grandfather's upright hand. Each entry had a temperature and a shelf sketch, and Anthony noticed that the pale clay never appeared on the same page as the red. Earthenware, one line read, below about 1,200. He flipped forward. Porcelain, another said, 1,200 to 1,400. Between those pages the loads split cleanly, like the notebook had been keeping two congregations apart on purpose.

He carried the notebook out to the porch, where his grandfather was sorting tomatoes into crates for the market. "Grandpa, why are these in different loads?"

His grandfather looked at the page, then at him. "Porcelain takes the hotter fire," he said. "The red clay stays under twelve hundred." He went back to the tomatoes.

That was all, and Anthony understood it was all he would get. His grandfather was a man of generous silences and calibrated understatement; his highest praise for a well-centered pot was "not the worst I've seen," and Anthony had learned by now that this was litotes, praise folded small so it would keep. The numbers, though, were not folded at all. Below about 1,200 for the earthenware, 1,200 to 1,400 for the porcelain, and no page where both appeared. If he stacked his grandmother's set into one firing, one of two things would happen, and neither was the set she wanted.

He sat on the porch steps with the notebook and thought about it as an argument between two loyalties. His grandfather would say fire them separately, two loads, two days, patience. His studio teacher in the spring had said something different, that a set wanted unity, one fire, one moment in the heat, so the glazes would marry. Anthony had liked that idea when he heard it. It felt less like a technique and more like a principle, and he had been collecting principles lately, the way other people collected ticket stubs.

But the notebook was evidence, and evidence outranked principle. He carried the cup and the bowl back inside and sequestered the porcelain cup on the top shelf of the kiln, alone, its pale wall catching the light from the peephole. The earthenware bowl he wrapped in the damp cloth and set on the board for the second firing, two days later. It meant the set would be finished the morning before he left for school instead of with a week to spare. It also meant the bowl would be a bowl and the cup would be a cup, and he found, standing there with his hand on the kiln lid, that he could not make himself regret the trade.

What he could not settle was whether unity came from the fire or from the hand. He turned the cup in his fingers and found the throw lines, four faint spirals his own thumb had left, and the same spirals in the bowl's wall. Same wrist, same summer, same afternoon of oak shadow on the board. Maybe that was the marriage. Maybe the two fires were only arithmetic, and the set was already one thing before it ever met heat. He held both answers the way he held the cup, loosely, willing to be wrong about either.

He programmed the controller himself, checking the notebook twice, and loaded the cup with the cones. His grandfather came out at dusk in his market clothes and stood beside the dark kiln with his hands in his pockets, listening to the elements begin their low hum.

"Not the worst load I've ever seen," he said, and went inside to wash up.

story:
The notice was taped to the door of Room 114 by second period: PRINT DEADLINE MOVED UP TO TONIGHT, 9 P.M., NO EXCEPTIONS. Amy read it twice, because the Flagler Messenger had never moved a deadline in the three years she'd been on staff, and because folded beneath the tape was a photocopy of an email from Mr. Dakos, owner of Dakos Family Diner, the paper's only paying advertiser. He had read last week's story about health-code violations in his kitchen, and he wanted it retracted, and he wanted an apology, and until then his three hundred dollars a month was, in his words, on hold.

The media studies classroom smelled like warm toner and the lemon floor cleaner the janitor used on Fridays. Mr. Vidal had assigned the room to the newspaper staff for the day, so twenty desks had been pushed into a rough horseshoe and Amy sat at the center of it, laptop open, the offending story on the screen. It was careful work: two health-inspection reports, an interview with a former dishwasher, a quote from a student who'd found a hair in her gyro. Nothing in it was false, as far as anyone could tell, which was exactly the problem, because you cannot retract a thing that happened.

"We pull the ads, we're a blog," said Marcus, the business manager, who kept the budget in a spiral notebook because he distrusted spreadsheets. "Three hundred dollars prints eight hundred copies. Without him we print three hundred and hand them out like pamphlets on a street corner."

"Then we print three hundred," Amy said.

"Then half the school doesn't read us at all."

That was the shape of the argument for most of fourth period, going around the horseshoe like a cold being passed from desk to desk. Priya thought they should soften the story online, take out the word "repeatedly." Devin thought they should run a follow-up so glowing it would "balance" the first one, a suggestion that made Priya laugh so hard she had to put her head on the desk. Someone suggested asking the student council for money, and someone else pointed out that the student council was currently refusing to fund anything except the homecoming fog machine, an obsession that had enraptured them since August.

During lunch Amy went back to the media studies shelf at the back of the room, mostly because Mr. Vidal's copy of a fat gray book with a coffee-ring on the cover had been nagging at her all morning. She'd skimmed a chapter from it in September, something about how news got made, and she remembered a phrase, or half a phrase, drifting around in her head like a song she'd heard through a wall. She found the page by luck, chapter one, and there it was, a list of what the authors called filters, five of them, things news passed through before it reached anyone. The first was ownership. The second was advertising. She read that section twice, slowly, while the cafeteria noise came faintly through the wall.

Outlets that depended on advertisers' money, the book said, had a reason to avoid coverage that drove those advertisers away. That was the whole of it, stated almost mildly, as if it were obvious. Amy sat with the sentence for a moment, turbid coffee from the teachers' machine going cold beside her, and felt the strange recognition of seeing your own life described in a book written thirty years before you were born. Dakos wasn't some media conglomerate. He sold gyros. But the mechanism, if that's what it was, looked exactly the same at any size: the money came from somewhere, and the money could leave.

At 5:30 the staff regathered in Room 114, and Amy stood at the whiteboard with a marker that was dying and had to be shaken between every third word. "Here's where we are," she said. "We have a story that's true, an advertiser who's angry, and a deadline at nine. And I found something in the Chomsky book on the shelf. He and another guy list these things called filters. The second one is advertising." She wrote the word on the board and underlined it. "Basically, if your money comes from ads, you have a reason to not run stuff that makes the advertisers leave."

"So we're... filtered," Devin said. "Right now. Us."

"Looks like it," Amy said. "The question is what we do about being inside the machine."

Priya said the honest answer was to run the story and let the paper die nobly, and she said it with such fervor that Marcus quietly pointed out that noble death was easy to advocate when your job wasn't the budget. He opened his spiral notebook to the page with the numbers, and for a while nobody spoke, because the numbers were not complicated and they were not on the side of nobility.

Amy kept thinking about the word "amalgam," which she'd learned in chemistry for a lab report and which kept applying itself to everything that afternoon. The paper was an amalgam, really: part public service, part class project, part small business with exactly one customer. You couldn't separate the parts cleanly, and maybe pretending you could was its own kind of dishonesty. She proposed a compromise to the horseshoe, and the room argued it into a shape everyone could live with: the story stayed, word for word, online and in print; the print run would be smaller; and on the back page, where Dakos's ad had run, they would print a box explaining that the paper was funded by advertising, listing what his three hundred dollars had paid for, and inviting any business that wanted to support independent student journalism to get in touch.

At 8:52, Marcus hit print from the old desktop in the corner, and the laser printer began its slow mechanical rumble, sheet by sheet, like something being reluctantly persuaded. Amy carried the warm first copies to the counter by the window while Priya read the back-page box aloud one last time, checking for typos, and the room went quiet again, the kind of quiet that comes after a decision rather than before one. Nobody knew yet whether anyone would answer the invitation, or whether Mr. Dakos would ever speak to them again, and Amy found she could hold both of those unknowns at once without her hands shaking. Outside, a groundskeeper was dragging the soccer goals across the dark field, one squeaking wheel at a time, and she stood watching him until the last copy came out.

story:
John had agreed to spend the last week of August at his grandmother's house on the understanding that it would be quiet, and for three days it had been, until she decided that his Advanced Placement summer assignment, a formal critique of a Frida Kahlo painting, required her participation. She had cleared the dining table herself, an act of such obstreperous energy that the sugar bowl rang against the cream pitcher, and set down a library book with a cracked spine, open to a reproduction of The Two Fridas.

"Two of her," John said, bending over the page. He had chosen the painting because it looked like something he could say a lot about, blue and red and white, symmetrical and yet not. Now that he had to write four hundred words on composition and symbolism, the choosing felt less clever.

His grandmother sat across from him with her coffee and did not offer an opinion, which was her way of offering one. John took out his notebook and began to sketch the basic arrangement, two women seated side by side holding hands, because his teacher had insisted that drawing the composition taught you things that looking did not. He was not good at drawing. The left Frida came out with shoulders like a coat hanger, and the right Frida's face looked, in pencil, like a stranger in a passport photo.

"The colours first," he said to himself, remembering the rubric. Cool tones in the background, stormy blues and grays. The Frida in white wore paler skin, the traditional Tehuana dress in the darker figure burned with warm reds and golds. He wrote down that the palette split the canvas in half, cold European side and warm Mexican side, then crossed it out because it sounded like a worksheet.

His grandmother leaned over and tapped the right-hand figure. "She looks like someone waiting for news."

"She's supposed to be the one Frida loved," John said. "The one on the left is the one he didn't want anymore." He knew the story from the textbook's margin note, though he was already suspicious of it, since it explained everything so conveniently, as if a painting were a diary entry with costumes.

He kept sketching, and it was the sketch that stopped him. To place the figures he had to draw the line between them, and the line was not a rope or a ribbon. Both women's chests were open, both hearts exposed, one whole and beating, one with the valves cut, and a single blood vessel connected them, winding down out of one heart, looped through their joined hands, and back up into the other. He traced it with his pencil twice, slowly, the graphite squeaking against the paper. "Grandma," he said, "look. The artery goes through their hands. That's how they're connected. It's not the hands holding, it's the vessel."

She put on her glasses and studied his crude drawing, then the reproduction. "So the one who was rejected is giving her blood to the other," she said. "Or taking it. You can't tell which way it flows."

That was the problem, and John felt it open under him like a trapdoor in a stage floor. His critique wanted a thesis, a claim about symbolism, and the painting would not choose. He could argue that the doubled figure was a divided consciousness, the self split by abandonment into two halves that could not be separated, one bleeding out and one kept alive by the same shared line. He could also argue the opposite, that the connection was a delusion, that the torn heart could not actually feed anything and the whole unity was painted optimism. He wrote both sentences in his notebook, one under the other, and could not make himself cross either out.

"You look like your grandfather when you're stuck," his grandmother said. "He'd walk away from the table, come back, and the thing would still be wrong, but he'd feel absolved of it anyway."

"Was he good at that?"

"He was excellent at it. I did the fixing." She reached over and turned the book a quarter turn so the two Fridas faced John directly. The stormy sky behind them went on churning, indifferent to both interpretations. John picked up his pencil and began to shade the torn heart, building up the graphite in careful layers, darker at the place where the vessel left it. He would send in the critique with both arguments and let his teacher decide whether that was weakness or honesty, and meanwhile he added a small note to his sketch: which way does it flow. His grandmother refilled her coffee and watched him work, and the sugar bowl, jostled one last time, rang out against the cream pitcher and was still.

story:
Eli had set his phone face-down on the table, which was allowed only because he had promised his mother it was "for a project." It was, technically. The project was this: at dinner he was going to prove to his father that the story about the harbor cleanup was wrong, and he had forty-one minutes before his father's phone buzzed and the argument moved on without him.

"It's a puff piece," Eli said, sliding his tablet beside the mashed potatoes. "The Ledger ran it like the terminal expansion is this huge environmental win. But the same company owns the terminal."

His father buttered his bread with the patience of a man who had heard this before. "The Ledger's been here sixty years. Your grandfather read it."

"Eating," his mother said, in the voice that meant continue, carefully.

Eli's sister Priya, home from her first semester of college, reached over and turned the tablet toward herself before their father could. "Where's the ownership listed?" she asked, not looking up. She had a way of joining an argument sideways, as though she were only curious, and by the time you noticed she'd taken your side or destroyed it, the plates were already being cleared.

"Page two of the annual report. Merrick Logistics. They bought the paper's parent company two years ago. Nobody wrote about it except one blog, and that blog's gone now."

His father set down his fork. "So what? Reporters don't check with the owner before they write."

"Some do." Eli had the second tab open before his father finished the sentence. This was the part he had found at eleven the night before, hunched at the kitchen counter while the dishwasher hissed. He turned the screen around. "Reporters Without Borders. They publish a World Press Freedom Index, they've done it since 2002, and they score a hundred and eighty countries." He scrolled. "We're not even in the top twenty."

"Language," his mother said automatically, though nothing needed censoring yet.

"It counts concentration of media ownership," Priya read, tilting her head. "As one of the pressures. So it's not just governments jailing journalists, it's six companies owning everything." She looked up at her father. "That's the thing you don't like about it, actually. It's not liberal or conservative. It's just counting."

Their father was quiet in a way that Eli had learned to watch for. The quiet could mean he was losing, or that he was about to win, and the two looked identical from the outside.

"So what do you want," his father said finally. "The paper to run a disclaimer on every story? 'Warning, owned by money'?"

"Maybe just the ones about the owner."

Priya laughed, and even their mother's mouth twitched, which Eli counted as a diplomatic victory.

Then his father did the thing he did, the pivot that made arguing with him like wrestling someone who kept changing weight. "Fine. Say you're right. Say Merrick leaned on them. You still read the story in the paper, and you still found the ownership filing in ten minutes on that thing. So the system worked. You didn't need the index to tell you to be skeptical."

Eli opened his mouth and closed it. Because that was partly true, and it annoyed him how partly. He had found the filing. But he had only looked because his civics teacher, an impecunious man who gave guest lectures for a small honorarium and rode a bike with a milk crate zip-tied to the rack, had once cajoled the class into spending twenty minutes a week checking who owned what they read. He had made it sound like a game. Eli had done it exactly twice before tonight.

"The system worked because one guy nagged me," Eli said. "That's not a system."

"It's the only system there is," his father said. "People nagging other people. Used to be your grandfather nagging me about the radio."

Priya put the tablet down between the salt and the green bean dish, screen still lit, the ranking still there like a witness who had finished testifying and was waiting to be dismissed. "He's right that you checked," she said to Eli, "and you're right that he only checked because somebody made it a habit. Both of those can be true."

"That's very college of you," their father said.

"Thank you. It cost forty thousand dollars."

Their mother stood to get the pie, which was her method of adjourning court. Eli still didn't know whether the Ledger's reporter had been told what to write or had simply known which stories kept his job safe, and he understood, watching his father carry his plate to the sink, that the index could count the owners but not that part. He picked up his phone and turned it over.

"Grandpa's coming Sunday," his mother said from the counter. "Don't start with him about the radio."

"Too late," said Priya. "Start with the pie."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
story:
The apartment smelled like fresh paint over old cigarettes, and Jayden's mother kept touching the kitchen counter the way she touched things she couldn't afford. The listing agent, a woman named Dolores with a lanyard and a clipboard, said the rent was fourteen hundred a month, plus a security deposit of one month's rent, refundable if they left the place in good condition. Jayden wrote it in his phone. Fourteen hundred, plus fourteen hundred up front, plus first month's rent before they even got keys. His after-school job at the garden center paid three hundred a week in summer, less now. He did the math standing in the empty living room while his mother asked about the lease term.

"Young man," Dolores said, catching him typing. "You calculating something?"

"Whether I can help," Jayden said. "Half of fourteen hundred is seven hundred. That's most of what I make."

His mother said his name in the tone that meant not now, but Dolores looked at him with something like approval, which felt better than it should have.

They had to move because their building was being sold, and their landlord, Mr. Ferreira, was planning to abscond to Arizona with whatever he'd made over twenty years of collecting their checks in person. That was how his mother put it, laughing, though Jayden could tell the laughing was circumlocution, a wide road around the fact that they had thirty days and nowhere to go. He had started studying. If they were going to pay rent forever anyway, he wanted to understand the whole machine, rent and deposits and the thing Mr. Ferreira used to mention called a mortgage, which was a loan for buying a place, paid back monthly over decades, and which required a down payment, a chunk of cash up front, usually some percentage of the price. He'd learned that much from the library's public computers. The rest he was assembling from adults who let things slip.

Marcus, his mother's friend from the hospital where they both worked, had slipped plenty. Three weeks ago, over paper plates of rice and beans, Marcus had been quiet and then suddenly loud about his house. "Same house, same bank, nothing changed," he'd said, jabbing his fork. "Payment went up two hundred a month this year." Jayden had asked how that could happen if nothing changed, and Marcus had said, "Adjustable-rate mortgage. That's what the bank called it. The rate moves. Fixed-rate, the rate stays put. Mine moves." He'd gone back to his beans, and Jayden had sat with the fork halfway to his mouth, recalibrating something. A house was not a fixed thing even when it was fixed in place.

Now, at the viewing, Dolores was saying the landlord of this building also owned a duplex he might sell. "You ever think about buying?" she asked his mother, almost casually. "First-time buyers, there are programs. Down payment assistance."

"With what?" his mother said, still kind, still smiling.

The question stayed in the air. Jayden looked at the window, at the parking lot below, at a man loading a stroller into a minivan. He thought about Marcus's two hundred dollars, how the payment could rise even when the person paying had done nothing, had planted the same flowers and mowed the same lawn. Rent went up too, at renewal, he knew that. But with the adjustable thing, it could climb without warning, following some index out in the market that no one in the kitchen had voted on. And with the fixed kind, it held. He tried to weigh them against each other and couldn't finish the weighing, because he didn't know what the market might do, and neither, he suspected, did anyone.

In the car afterward, his mother was quiet until the highway, and then she said, "You don't have to pay for anything, Jayden. That's my job."

"I know."

"I mean it. Seven hundred dollars, you're seventeen."

"I'm almost eighteen," he said. "And you work nights. I'm just doing arithmetic."

She drove with both hands on the wheel. Jayden watched her jaw move the way it did when she was deciding whether to say a thing, and he understood that her anger about the moving, about Mr. Ferreira, about all of it, was sitting underneath her offer like water under ice, and that refusing his help was the last piece of the old life she could still control. He thought of Dolores saying down payment assistance, which had sounded generous in the apartment and specious now, in the car, where the gap between assistance and enough was the whole of their situation.

"Marcus's payment went up because of the rate," Jayden said. "Adjustable kind. Nothing else changed, just that."

His mother glanced at him. "He told you that?"

"I asked. If we ever bought something, I'd want the fixed kind. At least I'd know the number."

She was quiet for two exits. Then she said, "The deposit on that place is a month's rent. Fourteen hundred. If I do the deposit and first month together, that's twenty-eight hundred, and I have nineteen." The numbers sat between them, plain and unhurried, more honest than anything either had said all day.

"I have six hundred saved," Jayden said. "From the garden center."

"Jayden."

"It's for this. It was always for this, I just didn't know it yet."

She pulled into the gas station by their old building, the one they had to leave, and cut the engine, and looked at him in the sudden quiet. The pump outside waited with its hose coiled. "Five hundred," she said. "You keep a hundred. And we're getting it in writing that you get it back when we're stable, with interest, like a real loan."

"Like a fixed-rate loan," he said.

She laughed once, a short sound, and put her hand on the gearshift. "Fixed-rate. Six percent, kid. Now go pump the gas."
