The phone store smelled of floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Sebastian had been standing at the counter long enough to memorize the ceiling tiles, forty-one of them, four stained. His own phone lay dark on the glass between him and the clerk, drowned in Tuesday's storm when he had run the half mile from the bus stop with it in his jacket pocket. He was leaving for college in the morning, eight a.m., a drive of six hours, and without a phone his mother had said it would be like sending him off with a paper map and a flare gun.

"Insurance claim first," the clerk said, typing. "Then the upgrade. You'll need to sign the terms and conditions before I can process anything, and we close at nine."

Sebastian signed the first screen without reading it, then stopped himself, thumb hovering. He was the kind of person who read the back of cereal boxes. He scrolled back up. The clause at the top ran for two paragraphs about liability, about how the company was not responsible for acts of God, and that phrase stopped him, because he had seen it somewhere else, recently, somewhere that mattered.

"My concert tickets," he said. He pulled the drowned phone toward him uselessly, then remembered and borrowed the clerk's display tablet instead. He logged into his email and found the message from the venue. The show, the one he had bought tickets for in June with money from mowing lawns, the one that was supposed to be tonight, had been canceled. The storm had taken part of the roof off the amphitheater. The email offered his money back as credit toward next season, and beneath that, in gray nine-point type, sat the sentence he had skimmed three days ago and not understood: per the force majeure provision of the ticket terms, no cash refunds would be issued.

"What's force majeure?" he asked the clerk.

The clerk glanced at the tablet and shrugged. "It's in every contract we have too. Force majeure frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, like a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing." He said it flat, the way he probably said it forty times a week, and went back to typing.

Sebastian read the clause again. The storm had prevented the venue from holding the concert; the venue had not chosen to cancel it out of laziness or greed, at least not provably. So the venue was freed from its obligation to put on a show, and, apparently, from its obligation to give him back his sixty dollars. He felt two reactions push against each other. One was simple indignation: he had paid for a concert, and there had been no concert, and money should travel backward along that broken promise. The other was a stranger, more reluctant feeling, an interest in how the machine worked, an almost admiring recognition that somewhere a lawyer had sat down and imagined storms and wars and roof failures in advance and written a door for the company to walk through.

"The thing is," he said slowly, "I get it. If a war started, you couldn't exactly demand the band play. It's not their fault." He turned the tablet toward the clerk. "But it's not my fault either. Why does the clause only open the door for them?"

The clerk looked up for real this time. "What's your major?"

"Undeclared. I leave tomorrow."

"Then take a law class." He slid a second screen across the counter. "Device payment agreement. You're financing three hundred dollars over twenty-four months. Read that one, actually. People always skim that one."

Sebastian read it. He read the part about consent, how signing indicated his agreement to be bound. He read the liability section, which capped the company's responsibility at the phone's purchase price. He read about arbitration, a word he liked the shape of without fully trusting it. Around him the store was emptying; a mother negotiated with a small boy over a case with cartoon dogs on it, and a delivery guy in a rain jacket waited for a screen repair, and the fluorescent lights hummed at a pitch that seemed designed to be ignored.

His mother texted from the demo phone's message relay, a service the clerk had set up out of what Sebastian suspected was pity: Are you getting it or not, we need to pack the car tonight. He noticed he was doing something he recognized from arguing with his father, which was holding two positions at once without collapsing them. The venue had behaved reasonably under a rule that was itself reasonable, and he had still lost sixty dollars, and both of those things were true, and neither one erased the other. He could not find a principle that made the loss fair. He could only find a principle that made the loss legal, and he was surprised, scrolling through the gray text, by how much distance could fit between those two words.

"Okay," he said, and signed. Then, before the clerk could take the tablet back, he opened the venue's website and found the contact form. He did not demand a refund. He wrote instead: I accept the force majeure terms. I'm asking for the refund anyway, as a courtesy, because I'm a student and the show would have been my last one before moving away. He hesitated over the word courtesy, worried it sounded like equivocating, and left it in, because it was honest: he did not know if he deserved the money, and he wanted it, and he was unwilling to pretend one of those feelings didn't exist.

"Smart," the clerk said, reading over his shoulder with the frankness of someone who had stopped caring about boundaries hours ago. "The folks who yell get form letters. The folks who quote the clause back at us get listened to." He boxed up the new phone, white and boxy in its shrink wrap. "You'll have it activated in ten minutes. Sign here, initial there."

Sebastian's pen moved through the boxes, his initials appearing one after another like a small procession, and he thought briefly of the word acolyte, which he had learned for the SAT and never used, and how he was signing his way into a church of terms he had only partially read. The phone came alive in his hand, screen bright, and the first message through was his mother's: I packed your rain jacket. Check the weather before you go. He looked out the store's front window at the drying parking lot, at the sky still bruised in the west, and then he checked.

story:
The suite smelled like buffalo sauce and wet coats, and Carson had exactly twenty-two minutes until the halftime trivia board lit up on the jumbotron, twenty-two minutes to decide whether his grandfather was a liar or just old. The contest had been announced at the end of the first quarter: one question per suite, answers texted in before the second half kicked off, and the prize was a locker room tour, which Carson wanted more than he had admitted to anyone, including himself.

"It was the Packers," Grandpa Ray was saying, wedged into the corner seat with a plate balanced on his knee like a man who had done this a hundred times. "Packers and the Chiefs. I remember it like yesterday." He was a gourmand of halftime spreads even now, working through the chicken wings with a methodical devotion, pausing only to gesture at the field below with a dripping bone.

Carson's mother rolled her eyes from across the room. "Dad, you were four in 1967." She said it lightly, the way she said most things about Grandpa Ray, but Carson had learned that lightness could carry weight, the way a paper airplane carries a stone if you fold it wrong.

"Five," Grandpa Ray said. "And I remember the score. Thirty-five to ten." He pointed the bone at Carson. "You think I make things up."

Carson didn't answer that, because the honest answer was sometimes, and the second honest answer was that he wanted Grandpa Ray not to have made this up. The trivia question had blinked onto the screen at the end of the first quarter: WHEN AND WHERE WAS THE FIRST SUPER BOWL PLAYED, AND WHAT WAS THE FINAL SCORE? His cousin Priya had already started typing "Green Bay" into the family's shared answer, because everyone knew the Packers were a Green Bay team, and something about that had snagged in Carson's mind like a sleeve on a nail. His grandfather had said Los Angeles. On the screen, the Chargers' kicker lined up for a field goal, and the whole suite went quiescent, even the twins, even the dog, waiting while the ball sailed wide left and the room broke into groans.

"Wait," Carson said, and Priya's thumbs stopped. "Grandpa, you said it was in Los Angeles. Not Green Bay."

"Of course it was in Los Angeles." Grandpa Ray looked faintly wounded, the way he did whenever anyone demanded evidence for his memories. "Big stadium out there. January. Cold everywhere else in the country but not there." He licked sauce off his thumb. "Fifteenth, I think. January fifteenth."

Priya was frowning at her phone. "That can't be right. Why would they play a Packers game in LA?" But she said it as a question, not a verdict, and Carson recognized the tone because it was his own, the little hitch before you commit to believing something. Fourteen minutes to kickoff of the second half. He thought about how they had all spent years humming to Grandpa Ray's stories, letting him have them the way you let a kid win at cards, and how it would be a strange kind of cruelty for this to be the one story that was true. It would also, he admitted to himself, be a strange kind of gift.

He got up and found his uncle Devin by the window, the one family member with actual data on his phone, the one who had made a small fortune in fantasy football and treated every dispute like a courtroom. "Uncle D. First Super Bowl. Don't tell me who told you what. Just look it up."

Devin looked at him for a long second, and Carson understood that his uncle had already heard the argument from across the room, and had already, probably, looked it up, because that was who Devin was. "You asking for Ray or for the trivia?"

"Both. Separately."

Devin turned the screen toward him. Carson stood transfixed by it for a moment, not because the information was dramatic but because it was ordinary, plain black text: January 15, 1967, Green Bay Packers 35, Kansas City Chiefs 10, Los Angeles. Every number where his grandfather had said it would be. Down on the field, the halftime crew was hauling the stage pieces into position, and somewhere a clock was running that Carson couldn't see.

He walked back and sat down next to Grandpa Ray without saying anything, then took Priya's phone and typed: January 15, 1967, Los Angeles. Packers 35, Chiefs 10. He hit send with nine minutes still on the clock, before he could think better of it, before he could weigh whether he was doing it for the locker room or for the old man. The answer could only be submitted once. Priya made a small sound of protest that trailed off into nothing.

The jumbotron flickered. Then, in letters ten feet tall: SUITE 114. CORRECT.

Grandpa Ray set down his plate. For a second he didn't say anything at all, just looked at the screen, and Carson watched his throat move.

"Told you," he finally said. "Like yesterday."

story:
The sled drill came at the end of every Tuesday practice, after the passing patterns had been run into the grass and the cones stood crooked where cleats had knocked them. Coach Reyes had three of them load the weighted sled and push it twenty yards as a unit, shoulders against the bar, and he stood at the far sideline with a stopwatch he never seemed to read. Dominic took his spot at the left end and waited for the whistle.

They were slow. Not just Tuesday but every Tuesday that September, slow in a way that didn't match how any of them moved alone. Dominic had watched Femi sprint the length of the field in the last minute of a match and arrive at the far post still furious with energy. He had watched himself, in the mirror of his own body, chase down a breakaway in the season opener and feel his lungs open like a door. Yet when the three of them leaned into the sled together, the thing crawled.

"Again," Coach Reyes said that Tuesday, and then, quieter, almost to himself, "You each push harder when I time you one at a time. I've been watching it for a month."

That night Dominic sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open, collating what he could find: a name, Ringelmann, which he typed into a search bar and then into another. He read slowly, twice. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone. Dominic read the sentence out loud to the empty kitchen, then copied it into the notebook he kept for calculus.

He brought it to Femi before Thursday practice, holding the notebook open between them on the bench. Femi read it with his shin guards still in his hands.

"Ringelmann," Femi said. "Never heard of him."

"He measured it. Rope, groups, 1913. Everybody pulls less when they're in the group." Dominic closed the notebook. "It's not just us being lazy. It's what happens."

"So what do we do about it?"

Dominic had thought about this on the walk over, past the tennis courts where the nets sagged and a single player served balls to no one. Part of him wanted to say that knowing was enough, that a named thing was a handled thing. Another part, older and more skeptical, suspected that a fact like this was less an answer than a description of the problem. "I don't know yet," he said. "Maybe we count our own steps. Maybe we agree that each of us is responsible for his own push, and nobody assumes the other guy is carrying it."

"Meaning we all secretly think the other two have it," Femi said. "That's kind of comforting, actually. I thought I was just getting soft."

The infield grass was still wet when Coach called the sled drill on Thursday. Dominic lined up at the left end again, with Femi at center and Elias, a junior who rarely spoke, at the right. Before the whistle, Dominic said, without turning his head, "Your own push. Don't worry about ours." He heard Femi laugh once through his nose.

The sled moved. Not beautifully, not like a machine, but it moved the way it moved when Coach timed them individually, and Dominic felt his own thighs burn in a way he recognized from the opener. Afterward, doubled over with his hands on his knees, he tried to be honest with himself about what had changed. Perhaps the words had. Perhaps only Tuesday's rest had, or the cool in the air. He wanted to credit the sentence in his notebook and could not entirely.

At the water table, Elias drank and then said, "Was that real, or did we just want it to be?"

"That's the problem," Dominic said. "I can't tell the difference yet."

Over the next three weeks, the question stopped being a project and became a small persistent habit of mind, the way a player keeps checking his shoulder. He noticed it in the matches too. When the team defended as a block, each of them seemed to run a half step less than he did when the play broke and only one man was back. It felt endemic to them, not a flaw anyone had chosen but something grown into the structure, the way the goalposts leaned very slightly toward the south end. Whether it could be cured, or only watched, he didn't know. Coach Reyes, who had a reactionary streak about anything that smelled of sports science, dismissed the stretch bands a trainer once suggested and kept his stopwatch in his pocket, so Dominic assumed the sled drill would continue exactly as it was, unmeasured, which in its own way suited him.

On the last Tuesday of the season, the air had the smell of cut grass going cold, and the light failed early enough that the far goal stood half in shadow. Coach called the drill a final time. Femi, Elias, and Dominic took the bar, and before the whistle, Elias said quietly, "Own push," as if reminding himself of a word in a language he was still learning.

They pushed. The sled hissed over the wet turf, and Dominic felt the bar hard against his shoulder, felt the specific and separate weight of his own effort, which was all he had ever been able to feel of anyone's. When it crossed the twenty-yard mark, Coach said nothing, and Femi straightened up and looked back along the track of flattened grass.

"Again?" he said.

story:
On the third day of model parliament, Layla discovered that her bill was nonsense. She had written it in one evening, eight clauses about banning vending machines that sold energy drinks in schools, and she had been proud of its moral clarity. Now Mr. Osei had posted every submitted bill on the classroom wall, and hers was next to a bill by Priya Raman, and Priya's looked like a legal document while Layla's looked like a persuasive essay with numbered paragraphs.

"Who's going to enforce it?" Priya asked when Layla sat down beside her at the long table by the window. "Clause four says schools shall not permit the sale of noxious beverages. What counts as noxious? What counts as a school? Does a sixth-form college count?" Layla said she'd fix the definitions, but fixing definitions turned out to be its own kind of quicksand. If she named specific drinks, the bill went stale the moment a new brand launched. If she named caffeine thresholds, she needed numbers she didn't have. She spent a full study period drafting and redrafting clause two and ended up with something longer and less clear than what she'd started with.

The next morning she found Priya in the library with her laptop open to the UK Parliament website. "Look at this," Priya said. "In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament." She turned the screen so Layla could read it herself. "That's why theirs look like that. There's a whole office of lawyers whose job is the writing. We're doing their part and the MPs' part." Layla felt something between relief and irritation: relief that the difficulty wasn't her personal failing, irritation that the simulation had quietly handed them a task that actual professionals spent careers learning.

What she couldn't stop thinking about, though, was what the lawyers' involvement meant for the arguing. In her draft, every clause had been an argument wearing a costume; clause four had existed to say energy drink companies were behaving badly. A drafter's clause, she realized, reading Priya's version, was supposed to be neutral enough that even an opponent could apply it honestly. That was a different kind of writing, almost a different kind of honesty. She wasn't sure which she trusted more.

The committee session on Thursday put the question to a test she hadn't expected. Marcus, playing the industry backbencher, moved to amend her bill so that "the Secretary of State may issue guidance on permitted beverages" instead of the outright ban. It was, Layla had to admit, beautifully drafted; it sounded like action while doing almost nothing, and she suspected the subterfuge was deliberate. "So you want to replace a rule with a suggestion," she said. Marcus smiled. "I want to replace a rule the House will vote down with a suggestion it might pass. Your bill loses everything. Mine saves half."

Layla looked down at her clauses, at the margin notes Priya had penciled in, and tried to hold both thoughts at once. The ban was the right policy; she still believed that. But a law that failed in division was only a gesture, and Marcus's hollow amendment was at least a law. Her mother, who had grown up somewhere that government felt like a thing done to you rather than by you, had taught her that a perfect law nobody passed was worth less than a small one that restrained somebody's worst impulse. Priya, whose parents marched and wrote letters and believed compromise was how you got subjugated slowly, thought the opposite. Layla had spent two years assuming one of them was simply correct.

She stood to speak. "I'll accept the amendment," she said, and the room reacted before she'd finished, Marcus triumphant, Priya stiffening beside her. "But I want clause six changed. If the Secretary of State issues guidance, schools have to publish whether they're following it. If it's only guidance, then let everyone see who ignores it." The chair called for objections; Marcus studied her for a long moment, tapping his pen against the desk, trying to find the trap in it, and she waited, not sure herself whether there was one.

The amended bill went to debate on Friday, then to its vote, and passed on a division of nineteen to eleven, with four abstentions. It would go to the model House of Lords, then, if it survived, to their teacher-as-monarch for royal assent, a stamp and a bell. Priya walked out with her without speaking until they reached the lockers.

"Half a law," Priya said. "You're satisfied with that?"

"I'm not satisfied," Layla said. "I'm not sure what I am." She closed her locker and held the folder with the printed bill against her chest. "Ask me after the Lords."

story:
The garden behind the food bank had been a parking lot two years ago, and it still looked like one trying to be forgiven. Xavier had signed up for the Saturday shift because his scholarship application wanted evidence of community engagement, forty hours minimum, and he had calculated that nine Saturdays at four hours each, plus travel, would preempt any awkward November scramble. He was good at that kind of arithmetic. His mother called it planning; his guidance counselor had used the word "extrinsic," in a tone that suggested she thought it was a diagnosis.

A woman named Ruth handed him gloves and a bucket and pointed at the raspberry canes along the fence. "Pick what's ripe. What's not ripe stays." Then she went inside to weigh people in at the desk, which was, Xavier gathered, where the real work happened. The garden was a sideline. Its produce went into the hampers as the fresh item, the single tomato taped to the top of the bag like a bow on a gift nobody had wanted to need.

He was not alone. A girl about his age was already halfway down the row, moving faster than him, her bucket ringing with fruit. "Dee," she said, without looking up. "You're the new one. Try to keep the canes from whipping back, they'll get you in the eye and then you'll be a liability, and Ruth makes you sign a form." She picked three berries to his one. She had, he learned by the third row, been coming since she was twelve, and she wanted, with a specificity that startled him, to run the whole operation someday. She'd drawn up a rotation schedule on graph paper. Ruth had said it was too complicated. Dee had not forgiven this.

Around ten, Ruth called them inside to pack hampers, because the Saturday line had backed up past the coat racks. The warehouse room smelled of cardboard and floor wax. Dee assigned him to the baby-food shelf without being asked to assign anyone anything, and he began assembling the small bright jars into groups of six, the way a laminated sheet instructed, then adding the juice boxes and the snack packs that went into any hamper flagged for kids.

He hadn't expected the flags. He'd imagined, he realized, a room of single men in windbreakers, the food-bank patron of the news segment, and instead the floor was loud with children doing the specific boredom of waiting, one boy conducting an invisible orchestra with a breadstick. He counted flags out of something to do with his hands while his mind idled. Nine hampers on the table. Six had the kid additions. He did it again on the next table. Eleven, seven.

"There's a thing," Dee said, not pausing, taping a tomato. "It was on the flyer from HungerCount, that's Food Banks Canada's report. In March 2025, in Canada, about a third of food bank visits were children. One in three." She said it flat, the way you'd say the mall closes at nine. She had clearly said it many times, to many new ones, and it had stopped being information to her and become something more like weather.

He kept packing. A woman at the desk argued gently with Ruth about the size of her family, and Ruth argued gently back, and the probity of the whole exchange sat strangely with him afterward, both of them so careful, as though honesty were a thing that had to be protected on both sides. He thought about his forty hours, the form in his backpack with its signature lines, and about Dee's graph paper, and he understood that he had walked in holding two completely different ideas of the same room. In one, the hours were the point and the garden was the setting. In the other, the tomato was the point and the hours were nothing. He was not sure the second idea, now that he had it, made the first one false. The scholarship was real. His mother's rent math was real. The forms existed whether or not he despised them.

But the flyer number was also real, and it was not going to be less real in November. He decided, sorting juice boxes, that he would come back after the forty hours were done, and that he was honest enough with himself to admit he did not yet know whether that was a promise or a prediction. Some things you couldn't know until Saturday came and you either showed up or didn't. He suspected that was the actual test, and that it was badly designed, and that it was still the test.

At noon the line thinned. Ruth gave them each a cheese sandwich and a peach, the excess of some donation, and Dee sat on the loading dock eating hers with her legs swinging, the rotation schedule sticking out of her back pocket where she'd shoved it. "You did okay," she said. "For a liability who hasn't signed the form." Xavier peeled his peach in one long strip, careful, the skin coming away whole, and set the bucket of raspberries down between them.

story:
The screen door banged twice behind Ryder before it settled, and he carried his laptop out to the porch where the afternoon heat sat on the fields like a lid. His grandfather's farm occupied the flat alluvial bottomland along the river, soil so dark it looked wet even in August, and from the porch Ryder could see the water moving slow and brown between the levee and the treeline. He set the laptop on the rail, opened the message thread with Dex, and read what he had typed. You always mess this up. We lose because of you. He had written it at midnight and had not sent it, and now, in daylight, he couldn't decide whether it was honest or just mean.

Inside, his grandfather was drying dishes with his good hand. The stroke had debilitated his left side two winters ago, leaving the arm stiff in its socket, and he had learned to pin a plate against his body with his elbow while he wiped it. He had coached the high school debate team in this county for thirty-one years. Ryder had come for the weekend partly to see him and partly, though he hadn't said so, to be somewhere without cell service in the house, so he would have an excuse not to answer Dex.

"Still hiding from that boy's message," his grandfather said, not a question. He nodded toward the porch. Grandma had gone to town for groceries. "Come sit. Tell me what he did."

Ryder told him. Dex was his partner in team debate, the better researcher and the worse speaker, and at the district semifinal Dex had frozen during the rebuttal, lost the thread, and dropped their strongest argument. Worse, he'd missed two practices the week before and shown up late to the third. "I have to tell him he's costing us," Ryder said. "Coach says the team's mine to run next year. If I can't say it, I'm not actually running anything."

His grandfather set down the plate. He was quiet for a while, looking out at the river, and then he said one sentence, the way he said most things now, sparingly, as if speech were rationed. "There's a psychologist named Gottman. He separates a complaint, which names a specific behavior, from criticism, which goes after the person." Then he picked up the next plate and went back to drying.

Ryder sat with that. He thought of his own note, the words he'd typed at midnight. You always mess this up. Always. That wasn't a behavior, that was a verdict on Dex himself, a whole character in two words. He tried rebuilding the sentence in his head. You missed practice twice before districts, and in the rebuttal you dropped our strongest argument. It sounded smaller. It sounded like something that had happened rather than something Dex was. He wasn't sure it would land any softer. He wasn't sure, either, whether softness was even the point, or whether the point was that Dex could actually do something about two missed practices and nothing at all about being a person who always messed up.

He typed the new version on the porch, deleted it twice, and typed it again. "In the semifinal you dropped the school-funding argument in rebuttal, and you missed both practices that week. Those two things are why we lost, not anything about you. Can we fix them before state?" He read it aloud under his breath, hearing his grandmother's old elocution lessons in his own cadence, the way she'd made him say vowels around a pencil at the kitchen table. He walked to the end of the driveway where the signal lived, held the phone up like a lantern, and pressed send.

The reply came fast, which meant Dex had been staring at his phone too. Not a text. A voice note, forty seconds long. Ryder stood in the gravel and listened. "I've been waiting all week for somebody to say it to my face," Dex said. "Coach told me you were getting the team and I figured you'd just replace me." Then a pause, wind on his end. "I missed those practices because my mom had a biopsy Tuesday and I couldn't sit in a room with fourteen-year-olds arguing about school funding. But I should've told you. Look, I already asked Coach if we could run a full rebuttal drill on Monday. Two hours. If you're not tired of me."

Ryder started typing a joke about never being tired of anyone who did the evidence cards, then stopped, because there was something underneath the voice note he hadn't expected. Dex had been doing the same arithmetic Ryder had, the same weighing of honest against cruel, and had come out silent. Ryder had almost come out cruel. That the two of them could stand on opposite ends of the same fear and both be wrong about the other was not something he had a sentence for yet, and he let it stay unresolved, standing there in the gravel, the sun going low and gold across the bottomland.

His grandfather was on the porch when he came back, watching the river. "Sent it?"

"Sent it."

"Good." His grandfather turned the good side of his face toward him. "Your grandmother's going to want the whole thing at dinner. Word for word."

story:
The party had moved to the backyard because the June wind had made the front steps impossible for photographs. Twice Amy's cap had lifted off her head while her uncle Marcus held his phone up and remonstrated with the sky as if weather could be argued into cooperation, and the second time it landed in the hydrangeas and came back with a smear of pollen across the tassel. She clamped it under her arm and carried it to the picnic table like something rescued.

"You could have worn it backward," said her cousin Devi, who was fifteen and had opinions about everything Amy wore. "Or pinned it. Everyone pins it."

"It's a borrowed cap," Amy said. "Nadia's. She graduates next year."

Inside, her grandmother was arranging the cake, a sheet cake with AMY in blue script that had begun to lean in the heat. Her grandmother was taciturn by nature and by long practice, and she communicated approval mostly through food, so the size of the cake, three layers of it, said more than most speeches. What she wanted, Amy had figured out years ago, was for Amy to take the scholarship to the state school, forty minutes away, close enough for Sunday dinners. She had never once said this. She said things like, "The dorms there, I hear the food is decent," and, "Your grandfather drove past it on Tuesday, said the campus looked tidy."

At the table Amy sat between her father and Devi, and the cap sat on the bench beside her, square and ridiculous, and she kept turning it over in her hands. Her father was telling the story of his own graduation, how his mother had cried into a paper napkin and then ironed it and kept it. Amy was only half listening. She had until Monday to commit, and the two letters were folded in the drawer upstairs, the state school and the one in Chicago, and every adult at this table had a vote they hadn't cast aloud.

"Why is it this shape?" Devi asked suddenly, reaching over and tipping the cap with one finger. "Honestly, it's the dumbest hat ever invented. It won't stay on. It's flat. It's a board."

Amy started to say she didn't know, and then stopped, because she did know, some stray fact from months ago surfacing. "It's called a mortarboard," she said. "Because it looks like the board bricklayers use to hold mortar."

"A bricklayer's hat," Devi said.

"Not the hat. The board. The flat thing they carry the mortar on." Amy set the cap upright on the table, its four points making a small square planet between the potato salad and the lemonade. "So it's a builder's tool. You graduate, and they put a bricklayer's board on your head."

Her grandmother looked at the cap for a long moment. "Your grandfather laid brick," she said. "Thirty years. He'd have liked that."

The table got quiet in the way it did when her grandfather came up. Amy's father passed the cake early, without ceremony, and slices went around, and Devi ate hers standing up, hovering near Amy's shoulder.

"Chicago has brick buildings," Devi said, too quietly for the adults. "That's not a sign, but it could be one."

"That's not how signs work."

"That's exactly how signs work."

Amy laughed before she could stop herself, and then her grandmother, who had heard everything, of course she had heard everything, set down her fork. "Your grandfather wanted Chicago," she said. "For himself. Never went further than Toledo." She looked at the cap again. "He sent money home instead. To his mother. For years. Called it reparation, though for what, he never said."

It was the longest sentence her grandmother had produced all afternoon, and afterward she went back to her cake, and everyone let her.

Amy picked up the cap and put it on, square and level, and walked to the middle of the yard where the wind could reach her. It caught the board immediately, tugged at it, and she held it down with one hand and turned to face the fence and the hydrangeas and the whole tilted, pollen-dusted afternoon. "Marcus," she called. "One more."

He came jogging with his phone already raised. Behind her, Devi shouted, "Smile like you've decided," and Amy stood there in the wind, hand flat on the mortarboard, and did not answer either way.

story:
Evan arrived at the mall twenty minutes early, which he decided was worse than arriving late, because now he had to stand near the fountain and pretend to be interested in his phone while his heart did something arrhythmic and embarrassing. Priya had suggested they meet at the arcade at noon. In his pocket he had two rolls of quarters, a folding of cash he had earned bagging groceries, and a plan he had rehearsed so many times it had worn smooth and lost its edges.

She showed up in a yellow jacket, spotted him, and waved with the whole arm, not the small polite wrist-wave. "You beat me here," she said. "That's suspicious."

"I wanted to claim the good air hockey table," Evan said. "There is a good one. It's the one where the blower isn't capricious."

"Capricious."

"Sometimes the puck just stops. Like it's bored."

They played air hockey first, and she beat him twice, both times by one point, which felt like a mercy she was extending rather than luck. Then they moved to the bowling alley on the third floor, where the mall's carpet turned from gray to a bruised purple and the shoe rental guy didn't look up from his phone. Evan paid for both of them before Priya could reach for her wallet, and she said, "Okay, but I'm getting snacks," and he understood this as a small treaty being signed, a consonance between what he wanted to do and what she would allow, and it made him glad in a way he couldn't have explained to his brother, who would have said he was overthinking a pretzel.

The first game they were both terrible, laughing at gutter balls, and the second game tightened. Priya turned out to be the kind of person who narrated her own failures in a sportscaster voice. Somewhere in the third frame of the tiebreaker, Evan realized his hands were shaking, and not from the sixteen-pound ball. His pulse was doing the thing it did before exams, a fast shallow drumming, and Priya was standing close enough that he could smell the chlorine from her morning swim practice, and the two sensations braided together so thoroughly he couldn't tell which one belonged to which.

"You're pacing," she said. "You've walked past the ball return four times."

"I'm strategizing."

"You're vibrating."

He rolled a strike on the ninth frame purely by accident, and she rolled one back at him on purpose, and now they were tied going into the last ball, and the alley had gone quiet around them in the specific way arcades and alleys do, all noise receding to make room for one moment. He picked up his ball. His heart was slamming. He told himself it was the score, the tie, the fact that losing in front of her was suddenly unbearable and winning in front of her was somehow more so.

She won. Her last ball clipped the headpin at an angle that took down everything, and she didn't gloat, which was somehow worse than gloating, and they walked out past the snack counter where she bought him soft pretzel twists to expiate her victory, tearing one in half and handing him the bigger piece.

"It's a real thing," Evan said. They were sitting on a bench outside the arcade now, and the words came out before he could inspect them. "Misattribution of arousal. Psychologists call it that. A racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person standing nearby."

Priya stopped chewing. "Where did you read that?"

"My brother's psych textbook. I was looking for why I couldn't sleep last night." He turned the pretzel in his hands. "So here's my problem. My heart rate was completely abnormal for bowling. And I don't know if that means I like you, or if you just happened to be standing next to me during a tense tiebreaker, and my body filed the evidence wrong."

Priya looked at him for a long moment, and then at the fountain, where coins caught the light like small drowned constellations. "That is the most romantic terrible thing anyone has ever said to me," she said.

"I'm not done. The theory says I could test it. Bowling again, sometime, with the same stakes and no you. If my heart stays calm, it was you." He took a breath. "But if I'm being honest, I already know I'd rather not know than not see you again, which I recognize is not how experiments are supposed to work."

She finished her pretzel and dusted the salt off her fingers onto her jeans. "So we're skipping the control group."

"We're skipping the control group."

"That's bad science," Priya said. She stood up, zipped her yellow jacket to the chin, and held out her hand as if they were closing a business deal. "Same time next Saturday. Bring more quarters."

Evan took her hand, and his heart did the thing again, cause unknown, and he let it.
